Helsinki-Vantaa airport aprons – individual targets over time

Sentinel-1 IW GRD · 231 acquisitions, 04 Nov 2025 – 31 Oct 2026 · tracks: A058 (51), A160 (50), D051 (50), D080 (49), D153 (31)

6862 targets were detected in total, a median of 25 per scene. They group into 76 recurring positions. The median detection density is 12.6 per km² on the aprons against 2.37 per km² in the surroundings.

Long stays

A long stay is a position that is occupied continuously for at least 10 days (up to one missed scene allowed, detected in ≥75% of scenes). Examples are aircraft parked for maintenance or storage. Snow piles and parked equipment also produce long stays, especially in winter. 70 long stays were found; the longest are listed below. Full list: long_stays.csv.

Validation

  • False alarms. On natural surfaces, where no target can be, the detector finds a median of 2.37 targets per km² per scene, against 12.58 per km² in the search area. If the search area produced false alarms at the same rate, about 19% of its detections would be false.
  • Position vs mapped gates. 40% of recurring positions lie within 80 m of a mapped gate, against 12% of random points in the search area (Mann–Whitney p = 3.4e-05).
  • Long stays vs optical. For a long stay, the object is present at the optical pass time too. In 25 of 48 long stays the position is brighter in Sentinel-2 during the stay than outside it (one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.55).

Cross-check with Sentinel-2

Sentinel-2 passes around 12:50 local time, between the radar's morning and evening passes. For every position and every cloud-free Sentinel-2 image (38 images), the radar passes just before and after the optical image are compared. Only cases where those two radar passes agree are scored. The optical test asks whether a white object (min(R,G,B) reflectance ≥ 0.45) lies within 25 m of the position.

optical: presentoptical: absent
radar: present531
radar: absent55438

When the radar says present, the optical image shows a white object in 14% of cases. When the radar says absent, it shows one in 11% of cases. Overall agreement is 84% over 529 pairs, but this mostly reflects how common "absent at both" is. A clear gap between the two percentages would confirm the radar detections. A small gap means the check cannot confirm them. Possible reasons: a gate can be occupied by different aircraft before and after the optical pass, white vehicles and markings also pass the optical test, and at 10 m a narrow-body fuselage is thinner than a pixel.

Method

  • σ⁰ VV+VH on a 10 m grid; per track, the empty background is each pixel's 10th percentile over time. Fixed structures are part of the background and are not detected.
  • Target pixel: ≥7 dB above background and ≥-2 dB absolute. A target is ≥2 connected pixels inside the apron polygons buffered by 20 m.
  • Detections from all scenes are linked within 40 m. Linked groups present in ≥5% of scenes are recurring positions. A position is "present" in a scene if any pixel within 25 m passes the pixel test.
  • False alarms: the same detector runs on a control area where no target can be. That is the vegetation from targets.control_area if it is set, otherwise dark natural surfaces in the reference ring. Taxiways and runways are excluded from it.

Caveats

  • At 10 m pixels (about 20 m resolution) the radar shows that a large object is present. It cannot identify the aircraft type or registration. Two aircraft parked next to each other can merge into one target.
  • Aircraft at contact gates touch jet bridges and the terminal, so the background there is bright and those aircraft are harder to detect than on remote stands.
  • Ground vehicles, de-icing rigs and snow piles also produce targets.
  • Radar passes happen only around 06–08 h and 18–19 h local time. Aircraft that turn around between passes are never seen.

Data: Copernicus Sentinel-1/-2 (ESA) via AWS Open Data; aprons and gates: Overture Maps / © OpenStreetMap contributors. Files: detections.csv, positions.csv, presence.csv, scenes.csv, long_stays.csv.
